title: Statistics for Analysts
tagline: Describe, estimate and test, with a working spreadsheet in every module
summary: Learn the statistics an analyst uses every week: describing data, spread, distributions, probability, sampling and confidence intervals, and relationships. Every module has a spreadsheet lab that checks your calculations.

modules.title: Describing data
modules.summary: Know what kind of data you have, and summarise it with the mean, median and mode.
modules.outcome: You can classify variables, choose the right average for the situation and explain why the mean and median can disagree.
modules.intro: Statistics begins with a simple question: what does this data look like? Before any test or model, an analyst summarises: what kind of data is it, where is its centre and how does it spread? This module covers the first two.

topics.title: Types of data
topics.html:
Data comes in kinds, and the kind decides what you may calculate. You cannot average a favourite colour.

Kinds of variable
KindMeaningExamplesUseful summaries
CategoricalGroups or labelsBlood group, city, phone brandCounts, percentages, mode
Numerical, discreteCounted, whole numbersSiblings, goals, ordersMean, median, counts
Numerical, continuousMeasured on a scaleHeight, time, temperatureMean, median, spread

Within categories, an ordinal variable has a natural order (small, medium, large; rating 1 to 5) while a nominal one does not (colours). Numbers used as labels, such as roll numbers or phone numbers, are really categorical: averaging them is meaningless.

Watch out

Always ask what a number means before you average it. The average of PIN codes tells you nothing.

Try it yourself: Is the number of items in a shopping basket discrete or continuous?

Model answer. Discrete: you count whole items.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is continuous?
  • Number of pets
  • Weight of a bag (correct)
  • Shoe colour
  • Roll number

Weight is measured and can take any value in a range.

2. Which summary suits categorical data?
  • Mean
  • Standard deviation
  • Counts and percentages (correct)
  • Correlation

For groups you count how many fall in each.
keyPoints: Categorical data is groups; numerical data is counted or measured.
Numbers used as labels are not real numbers for averaging.

topics.title: Mean, median and mode
topics.html:
Formula · Mean

mean = (sum of values) / (number of values)

In a sheet: =AVERAGE(range).

Three averages
MeasureHow to find itBest when
MeanAdd all and divide by the countData is roughly symmetric, with no extreme values
MedianThe middle value after sortingData is skewed or has outliers
ModeThe most frequent valueCategories, or the most common value matters
Worked example

Salaries in a small firm

Salaries (thousands a month): 24, 26, 25, 27, 26, 28, 25 and 90.

  1. Total: 271, count 8, so the mean is 33.9.
  2. Sorted: 24, 25, 25, 26, 26, 27, 28, 90. The middle two are 26 and 26, so the median is 26.
  3. Seven of eight people earn between 24 and 28, so the median describes them better than the mean.

Answer. One very high value pulls the mean up. The median stays close to the typical person.

Tip

When the mean is far above the median, the data is skewed to the right, as incomes and house prices usually are.

Check what you just learned

1. Which average resists extreme values best?
  • Mean
  • Range
  • Sum
  • Median (correct)

The median depends only on the middle of the data.

2. The mode of 2, 3, 3, 4, 3, 5 is:
  • 3 (correct)
  • 2
  • 4
  • 5

3 appears three times.
keyPoints: Mean uses every value; median is the middle; mode is the most frequent.
A gap between mean and median signals skewed data or outliers.

topics.title: Percentages, percentiles and quartiles
topics.html:
A percentage compares a part with a whole. A percentile says what share of the data lies below a value: if you scored at the 90th percentile, 90% of people scored lower.

Quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts
NameMeaning
Q1 (25th percentile)A quarter of values lie below
Q2 (median)Half lie below
Q3 (75th percentile)Three quarters lie below
IQRQ3 minus Q1: the spread of the middle half
Worked example

Find the quartiles by hand

Sorted marks: 40, 45, 52, 58, 63, 70, 75, 82.

  1. Median: between 58 and 63, so 60.5.
  2. Lower half 40, 45, 52, 58: median 48.5, so Q1 = 48.5.
  3. Upper half 63, 70, 75, 82: median 72.5, so Q3 = 72.5.
  4. IQR = 72.5 - 48.5 = 24.

Answer. The middle half of students scored within a 24-mark range, a measure of spread that ignores extremes.

Tip

In a spreadsheet you can find Q1 and Q3 by applying MEDIAN to the lower half and the upper half of the sorted data.

Check what you just learned

1. A student at the 80th percentile scored:
  • 80 marks
  • Higher than 80% of students (correct)
  • Lower than 80%
  • Exactly average

Percentile is about position within the group.

Key terms: flip and sort

Categorical
Data in groups
Discrete
Counted numbers
Continuous
Measured numbers
Mean
Total divided by the count
Median
The middle value
Mode
The most frequent value
Quartile
A cut point dividing sorted data into quarters
keyPoints: A percentile tells you the share of data below a value.
IQR is Q3 minus Q1 and ignores extremes.

modules.title: Spread and variation
modules.summary: Measure how spread out data is with range, variance, standard deviation and z-scores.
modules.outcome: You can calculate variance and standard deviation step by step, interpret them and compare values on different scales with z-scores.
modules.intro: Two classes can have the same average mark and be completely different: one where everyone scored about 60, another where half scored 30 and half scored 90. Spread is what separates them.

topics.title: Range and interquartile range
topics.html:
The simplest measure of spread is the range: largest minus smallest. It is quick but fragile: one extreme value changes it completely. The interquartile range (IQR) is steadier because it ignores the extremes.

Two spread measures
MeasureFormulaWeakness
Rangemax - minDepends on two values only
IQRQ3 - Q1Ignores the tails entirely
Worked example

Same mean, different spread

Class A marks: 58, 60, 60, 62. Class B marks: 30, 50, 70, 90.

  1. Both means are 60.
  2. Range A = 4; range B = 60.
  3. Class A is consistent; class B is mixed.

Answer. The mean alone hides the difference: spread must be reported with it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which spread measure is least affected by one extreme value?
  • Range
  • Maximum
  • IQR (correct)
  • Sum

The IQR ignores the tails.
keyPoints: Range is max minus min; IQR is Q3 minus Q1.
Report a measure of spread together with the average.

topics.title: Variance and standard deviation
topics.html:
Formula · Sample variance

s squared = sum of (x - mean) squared / (n - 1)

The standard deviation s is the square root of the variance, so it is in the same units as the data.

Worked example

Six readings

Readings: 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 10.

  1. Mean = 36 / 6 = 6.
  2. Deviations: -2, 2, 0, -1, -3, 4.
  3. Squares: 4, 4, 0, 1, 9, 16, sum 34.
  4. Variance = 34 / 5 = 6.8; standard deviation = square root of 6.8 = 2.61.

Answer. A typical reading is about 2.6 away from the mean of 6.

Why n minus 1? A sample varies a little less than the whole population, so dividing by n slightly underestimates the spread. Using n minus 1 corrects that. In a spreadsheet, STDEV and VAR already do this.

Tip

A rough guide: in bell-shaped data most values lie within two standard deviations of the mean.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are deviations squared?
  • To make them bigger
  • To round them
  • To save time
  • So positives and negatives cannot cancel (correct)

Without squaring the deviations would sum to zero.

2. The standard deviation has the same units as:
  • The data (correct)
  • The variance
  • Nothing
  • Percentages

It is the root of the variance, back in the original units.
keyPoints: Standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean.
Use n minus 1 for a sample; STDEV does this for you.

topics.title: Z-scores
topics.html:
Formula · Z-score

z = (value - mean) / standard deviation

It says how many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean.

Reading a z-score
zMeaning
0Exactly average
+1One standard deviation above the mean
-2Two standard deviations below: fairly unusual
beyond +/-3Very unusual: check for an error or outlier
Worked example

Two tests, one comparison

Asha scored 78 on a maths test (mean 70, SD 8). Her friend scored 82 in English (mean 76, SD 3).

  1. Asha: z = (78 - 70) / 8 = 1.0.
  2. Friend: z = (82 - 76) / 3 = 2.0.
  3. Her friend did relatively better compared with their own class.

Answer. Z-scores put different scales side by side.

Try it yourself: A value is exactly one standard deviation below the mean. What is its z-score?

Model answer. -1.

Check what you just learned

1. A z-score of -2 means:
  • Two above the mean
  • Two standard deviations below the mean (correct)
  • Average
  • A mistake

The sign gives the direction.

Key terms: flip and sort

Range
Largest minus smallest
IQR
Q3 minus Q1
Variance
Average squared distance from the mean (n minus 1)
Standard deviation
Square root of the variance
Z-score
Distance from the mean in standard deviations
keyPoints: z = (value - mean) / SD.
Z-scores let you compare values from different scales.

modules.title: Distributions and the normal curve
modules.summary: Picture the shape of data with frequency tables and histograms, and use the normal curve to judge how unusual a value is.
modules.outcome: You can build a frequency table, read a histogram, describe skew and use the 68-95-99.7 rule.
modules.intro: Numbers summarise; shapes explain. A histogram shows at a glance whether data is symmetric, skewed, or has two peaks. The normal distribution is the most important shape in statistics because so many measurements follow it.

topics.title: Frequency tables and histograms
topics.html:
A frequency table counts how many values fall in each band. A histogram draws those counts as touching bars, so the shape of the data appears.

Marks of 20 students grouped in bands
BandStudents
Below 501
50 to 592
60 to 695
70 to 796
80 to 894
90 to 992

Choosing bands

  1. Use equal-width bands that do not overlap.
  2. Five to twelve bands suit most data sets.
  3. Say clearly whether the upper end is included, such as 60 to under 70.
  4. Check the counts add up to the total.
Tip

In a spreadsheet, COUNTIF at or above a start minus COUNTIF at or above the next start gives the count for one band.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the purpose of a histogram?
  • To list names
  • To find the mean exactly
  • To show the shape of the data (correct)
  • To round values

It reveals the distribution's shape.
keyPoints: A frequency table counts values per band; a histogram draws it.
Use equal, non-overlapping bands and check the total.

topics.title: The normal distribution
topics.html:
The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve. Heights, exam marks and measurement errors often follow it. It is fully described by two numbers: the mean (its centre) and the standard deviation (its width).

The 68-95-99.7 rule
WithinShare of values
1 standard deviation of the meanAbout 68%
2 standard deviationsAbout 95%
3 standard deviationsAbout 99.7%

How much lies near the mean

Choose a mean and standard deviation and see the range that holds about 95% of values.

Adjust Mean, Standard deviation and see Lower limit (mean minus 2 SD), Upper limit (mean plus 2 SD), Range holding about 95% of values change.

Worked example

Exam marks

Marks are roughly normal with mean 70 and SD 8.

  1. About 68% of students scored between 62 and 78.
  2. About 95% scored between 54 and 86.
  3. A mark of 94 is three SDs above the mean: very rare.

Answer. The rule gives a quick feel for what is typical and what is unusual.

Watch out

Not all data is normal. Incomes, queue times and city sizes are usually skewed. Always look at the histogram before you use the rule.

Check what you just learned

1. About what share of normal data lies within two standard deviations of the mean?
  • 50%
  • 68%
  • 100%
  • 95% (correct)

About 95%.

2. Which two numbers describe a normal distribution?
  • Mean and standard deviation (correct)
  • Mode and range
  • Median and IQR
  • Min and max

Centre and width.
keyPoints: A normal curve is set by its mean and standard deviation.
About 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs.

topics.title: Skew and outliers
topics.html:
Shapes you will meet
ShapeWhat it meansMean versus median
SymmetricBalanced either sideAbout equal
Right (positive) skewA long tail of high values (incomes)Mean above median
Left (negative) skewA long tail of low values (easy exam marks)Mean below median
Two peaksTwo groups mixed togetherNeither describes either group

An outlier is a value far from the rest. Do not delete it just because it is awkward. First ask: is it an error (a typed 900 instead of 90), or a real extreme (an outstanding result)? Errors are fixed; real values are reported, with the analysis shown both with and without them.

Dealing with an outlier

  1. Check the source: was it typed or measured wrongly?
  2. If it is an error, correct it; if not, keep it.
  3. Report the median and IQR, which resist outliers.
  4. Show the result with and without the outlier.

Check what you just learned

1. In right-skewed data the mean is usually:
  • Below the median
  • Above the median (correct)
  • Equal to the median
  • Zero

High values pull the mean up.

Key terms: flip and sort

Frequency
How many values fall in a band
Histogram
A chart of frequencies
Normal distribution
The symmetric bell curve
Skew
A lopsided shape with a long tail
Outlier
A value far from the others
keyPoints: Right skew puts the mean above the median.
Investigate outliers before removing anything.

modules.title: Probability
modules.summary: Work with chance: simple rules, conditional probability and expected value.
modules.outcome: You can calculate probabilities with the addition and multiplication rules, handle conditional probability from a table, and find an expected value.
modules.intro: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It is the bridge from describing data to making statements about the world beyond the data.

topics.title: Basic rules of probability
topics.html:
Formula · Probability of an event

P(event) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes

For a fair die, P(even number) = 3 / 6 = 0.5.

Rules
RuleFormulaUse when
ComplementP(not A) = 1 - P(A)It is easier to find the chance it does not happen
Addition (or)P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)Either event is enough
Multiplication (and)P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) for independent eventsBoth events must happen and do not affect each other
Worked example

Two dice

What is the chance of getting a six on both of two fair dice?

  1. The throws are independent.
  2. P(six) = 1/6 each time.
  3. P(both six) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36.

Answer. About 2.8%. Independent events multiply.

Common mistakes

  • Adding probabilities of independent 'and' events.
  • Forgetting to subtract the overlap in an 'or' question.
  • Assuming a coin is more likely to land tails after four heads in a row: each throw is independent.

Check what you just learned

1. P(not A) equals:
  • P(A)
  • P(A) squared
  • 1 minus P(A) (correct)
  • 0

The complement rule.

2. The chance of two heads in two fair coin tosses is:
  • 1/2
  • 1
  • 1/3
  • 1/4 (correct)

1/2 times 1/2.
keyPoints: Probabilities run from 0 to 1.
'Or' adds (minus the overlap); 'and' multiplies for independent events.

topics.title: Conditional probability from a table
topics.html:
A conditional probability is the chance of something given that something else is already known: P(A given B). Restrict your attention to the cases where B is true, then see what share also have A.

A survey of 200 students
Plays sportDoes notTotal
Uses a bike503080
Does not use a bike4080120
Total90110200
Worked example

Reading the table

What is the probability a student plays sport, given that they use a bike?

  1. Look only at the bike row: 80 students.
  2. Of them, 50 play sport.
  3. P = 50 / 80 = 0.625.

Answer. Among cyclists, 62.5% play sport, against 90 / 200 = 45% overall: the two are linked.

Try it yourself: Using the table, what is P(uses a bike given plays sport)?

Model answer. 50 out of the 90 who play sport: 50 / 90, about 0.56.

Tip

The order matters: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are usually different.

Check what you just learned

1. P(A given B) means:
  • The chance of A among cases where B is true (correct)
  • The chance of A and B
  • The chance of B
  • Always 0.5

Restrict to B, then look at A.
keyPoints: Conditional probability looks only at the cases where the condition holds.
P(A given B) is not the same as P(B given A).

topics.title: Expected value
topics.html:
Formula · Expected value

E = sum of (value x probability)

The long-run average result of repeating a chance process many times.

Worked example

A fair-ground game

A game costs 10 rupees. Outcomes (net gain): lose 10 with probability 0.5; win 5 with 0.3; win 20 with 0.15; win 100 with 0.05.

  1. -10 x 0.5 = -5.
  2. 5 x 0.3 = 1.5.
  3. 20 x 0.15 = 3.
  4. 100 x 0.05 = 5.
  5. Sum = 4.5 rupees.

Answer. On average a player gains 4.5 rupees a game. Real games are set so the expected value is negative for the player.

Expected value does not predict one game: you will never win exactly 4.5 rupees. It describes what happens on average across many plays, which is what insurers, casinos and decision-makers care about.

Watch out

Do not confuse expected value with the most likely outcome. In the game above the most likely outcome is losing 10 rupees.

Check what you just learned

1. A bet pays 6 with probability 0.5 and loses 2 otherwise. The expected value is:
  • 4
  • 2 (correct)
  • 1
  • 6

6 x 0.5 + (-2) x 0.5 = 2.

Key terms: flip and sort

Probability
A number from 0 to 1 for how likely an event is
Independent events
One does not change the other's chance
Conditional probability
The chance of A given B
Expected value
The long-run average of a chance process
keyPoints: Expected value is the sum of value times probability.
It describes the long-run average, not a single result.

modules.title: Sampling and estimation
modules.summary: Learn from a sample: how to choose one fairly, and how to put a margin of error on an estimate.
modules.outcome: You can recognise sampling bias, calculate a standard error and a 95% confidence interval and see how sample size affects precision.
modules.intro: We rarely measure everyone. We measure a sample and use it to say something about the whole population. This is powerful, but only if the sample is fair, and only if we say honestly how uncertain we are.

topics.title: Populations, samples and bias
topics.html:
Definition

Population and sample. The population is everyone or everything you want to learn about. A sample is the part of it you actually measure.

Sampling methods
MethodHow it worksGood for
Simple randomEveryone has an equal chanceSmall, listed populations
SystematicEvery k-th item from a listLong lists
StratifiedRandom samples from each groupGroups differ and all matter
ConvenienceWhoever is easy to reachRarely good: usually biased

Common sources of bias

  • Selection bias: some people are more likely to be chosen.
  • Non-response: those who answer differ from those who do not.
  • Self-selection: only motivated people volunteer for a poll.
  • Leading questions: the wording pushes an answer.
Watch out

A big biased sample is worse than a small fair one: it gives a precise wrong answer.

Check what you just learned

1. Which sampling method is most likely to be biased?
  • Simple random
  • Stratified
  • Convenience (correct)
  • Systematic

Whoever is easy to reach is rarely representative.
keyPoints: A sample must represent the population.
Convenience and self-selected samples are usually biased.

topics.title: Standard error and confidence intervals
topics.html:
Formula · Standard error of a mean

SE = s / square root of n

It measures how much sample means vary from sample to sample.

Formula · 95% confidence interval for a mean

mean plus or minus 1.96 x SE

Valid for reasonably large samples (about 30 or more) from roughly normal data.

Worked example

Study time

36 students: mean 52 minutes a day, SD 12.

  1. SE = 12 / square root of 36 = 2.
  2. Margin of error = 1.96 x 2 = 3.92.
  3. Interval: 52 plus or minus 3.92, so 48.08 to 55.92.

Answer. We are 95% confident the true mean lies between about 48 and 56 minutes.

The confidence level is a statement about the method: if we repeated the survey many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true mean. It is not the probability that this one interval is right.

How sample size shrinks the margin

Keep the spread fixed and watch the margin of error as the sample size changes.

Adjust Standard deviation, Sample size and see Standard error, Margin of error (95%) change.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens to the margin of error if the sample size grows?
  • It grows
  • It becomes zero
  • It stays the same
  • It shrinks (correct)

More data gives more precision.

2. With SD 10 and n = 25 the standard error is:
  • 2 (correct)
  • 0.4
  • 10
  • 5

10 divided by 5.
keyPoints: SE is s over the square root of n; the 95% margin is 1.96 SE.
A confidence interval describes the method, not one result.

topics.title: How big a sample do you need?
topics.html:
Precision costs data. To halve the margin of error you need four times as many people, because the margin depends on the square root of n.

Margin of error for a mean with SD 12
Sample sizeStandard errorMargin (95%)
252.404.70
1001.202.35
4000.601.18
16000.300.59
Tip

Decide in advance the margin you can accept, then work backwards to the sample size: n is about (1.96 x SD / margin) squared.

Watch out

A larger sample cannot fix bias. It only reduces random error.

Check what you just learned

1. To halve the margin of error you need:
  • Twice the sample
  • Four times the sample (correct)
  • Ten times the sample
  • The same sample

The margin depends on the square root of n.

Key terms: flip and sort

Population
Everyone you want to learn about
Sample
The part you measure
Bias
A systematic error in the sample
Standard error
How much sample means vary
Confidence interval
A range likely to contain the true value
Margin of error
Half the width of the interval
keyPoints: Four times the sample halves the margin of error.
More data cannot repair a biased design.

modules.title: Relationships and testing
modules.summary: Measure how two variables move together, fit a line and understand what a significance test is really asking.
modules.outcome: You can calculate and interpret correlation, build a line of best fit for prediction and explain the logic of hypothesis testing in plain language.
modules.intro: Analysts are rarely asked only to describe: they are asked whether two things are related, and whether a difference is real or just chance. This final module introduces the tools and the cautions that go with them.

topics.title: Correlation
topics.html:
The correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a straight-line relationship, from -1 (perfect fall) to +1 (perfect rise). 0 means no straight-line pattern.

Reading r
rMeaning
0.9 to 1.0Very strong positive
0.5 to 0.9Moderate to strong positive
-0.2 to 0.2Almost none
-0.5 to -0.9Moderate to strong negative
Watch out

Correlation is not causation. Two things can move together because a third thing drives both, or by coincidence. Always plot the data: a curve can have r near zero and still be a perfect relationship.

Worked example

Revision and marks

Hours of revision against exam marks for eight students give r of about 0.99.

  1. Strong positive: more revision goes with higher marks.
  2. That does not prove revision causes the marks: motivated students may do both.
  3. A study that assigns revision at random could test cause.

Answer. Correlation tells you that a link exists, not why.

Check what you just learned

1. r = -0.9 suggests:
  • A strong rise together
  • No relationship
  • A strong inverse relationship (correct)
  • Perfect

Strong and negative.

2. Correlation shows:
  • A cause
  • A prediction
  • Nothing
  • A link, not necessarily a cause (correct)

It does not prove cause.
keyPoints: r runs from -1 to +1.
Correlation does not prove causation; always plot the data.

topics.title: A line of best fit
topics.html:
The regression line is the straight line that fits the points best, with equation y = a + bx. The slope b says how much y changes for each one-unit rise in x; the intercept a is the predicted y when x is zero.

Formula · The line

y = intercept + slope x x

In a sheet: =INTERCEPT(known_y, known_x) + SLOPE(known_y, known_x) * x

Worked example

Predict a mark

The line for hours (x) and marks (y) has slope about 5 and intercept about 39.

  1. For 5.5 hours: 39 + 5 x 5.5 = 66.5.
  2. The line says each extra hour of revision goes with about 5 more marks.
  3. Only predict inside the range of the data you have: 20 hours may not follow the pattern.

Answer. Predictions are reliable inside the range of the data and risky outside it.

Common mistakes

  • Predicting far beyond the range (extrapolating).
  • Treating the slope as a causal effect.
  • Ignoring a curved pattern in the plot.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the slope tell you?
  • The change in y for each unit of x (correct)
  • The average
  • The spread
  • The sample size

It is the rate of change.
keyPoints: The slope is the change in y per unit of x.
Do not extrapolate far beyond the data.

topics.title: The logic of a significance test
topics.html:
A test begins with a null hypothesis (nothing is going on, for example the new method makes no difference). It asks how likely we would be to see data at least this extreme if the null were true. That probability is the p-value.

Reading a p-value
p-valuePlain reading
Small (below 0.05)The data would be rare if there were no effect, so there is evidence of an effect
LargeThe data are consistent with no effect; this is not proof there is none

Cautions

  • A p-value is not the probability the null is true.
  • Statistically significant does not mean important: check the size of the effect.
  • A small study can miss a real effect; a huge study can flag a trivial one.
  • Testing many things finds false alarms: report how many you tried.
Tip

Always report the size of the difference and its confidence interval alongside any p-value.

Check what you just learned

1. A small p-value means:
  • The null is certainly false
  • The data would be unusual if there were no effect (correct)
  • The effect is large
  • The sample is small

It measures surprise under the null.

2. Which should you report with a test?
  • Only the p-value
  • Nothing
  • The effect size and a confidence interval (correct)
  • The sample colour

Significance without size is incomplete.
